units.title: Linear algebra: determinants, systems and eigenvalues
units.subject: Engineering Mathematics
units.objective: Write AX=b using one fixed variable order. For a 2×2 matrix [[a,b],[c,d]], det(A)=ad−bc. Nonzero determinant permits an inverse and a unique solution for every right-hand side.
units.review: Original worked lesson with author checks. No independent human editorial review; not a complete exam chapter.

concepts.title: Start with the equations
concepts.text: Write AX=b using one fixed variable order. For a 2×2 matrix [[a,b],[c,d]], det(A)=ad−bc. Nonzero determinant permits an inverse and a unique solution for every right-hand side.

concepts.title: Do not infer too much from singularity
concepts.text: A zero determinant rules out an inverse but does not by itself distinguish no solutions from infinitely many. Compare equation consistency or use row reduction.

concepts.title: Check a candidate eigenpair
concepts.text: A nonzero vector v is an eigenvector only when Av=λv. For the original diagonal matrix diag(3,5), the coordinate directions have eigenvalues 3 and 5; a general vector combining both directions is not an eigenvector.

example.problem: Solve 2 x+y=7 and x−y=2. Check whether the coefficient matrix is invertible.
steps: Use variable order (x,y), giving A=[[2,1],[1,−1]].
det(A)=2(−1)−1(1)=−3, so the system has a unique solution.
Add the two equations: 3 x=9, hence x=3.
Substitute into x−y=2: y=1; both original equations hold.

recall: What does a nonzero determinant establish?
What remains unresolved when a determinant is zero?
Why must an eigenvector be nonzero?
units.mistake: A matrix and its transpose can share a determinant without having the same eigenvectors. Always verify the specified vector by multiplication.

units.title: Calculus: derivatives and signed accumulation
units.subject: Engineering Mathematics
units.objective: A derivative describes local rate of change; a definite integral gives signed accumulation. Include the variable and units before applying a rule.
units.review: Original worked lesson with author checks. No independent human editorial review; not a complete exam chapter.

concepts.title: State the quantity
concepts.text: A derivative describes local rate of change; a definite integral gives signed accumulation. Include the variable and units before applying a rule.

concepts.title: Differentiate before substituting
concepts.text: For f(x)=x³−2 x, f′(x)=3 x²−2. At x=2 the slope is 10. Substituting x=2 before differentiating turns the expression into a constant and destroys the required rate.

concepts.title: Check accumulated units
concepts.text: For an original velocity v(t)=2 t m/s on 0≤t≤3 s, displacement is ∫0³2 t dt=9 m. If velocity changes sign, displacement and total distance need not agree.

example.problem: A particle has position s(t)=t³−3 t metres. Find its instantaneous velocity at t=2 s and displacement from t=0 to t=2 s.
steps: Differentiate: v(t)=3 t²−3 m/s.
Calculate endpoint positions: s(2)=8−6=2 m and s(0)=0.
Displacement is 2−0=2 m; this is not the same quantity as final velocity.

recall: What is held variable before differentiation?
When can distance differ from displacement?
What units does integrating a rate produce?
units.mistake: A derivative at a point is not a finite interval average. Endpoint subtraction of position gives signed displacement, not necessarily path length.

units.title: Control systems: first-order response and feedback
units.subject: Control Systems
units.objective: The transfer-function model G(s)=K/(τs+1) below assumes zero initial state and τ>0. Its pole is −1/τ. Initial stored energy adds a response that the zero-state formula does not include.
units.review: Original worked lesson with author checks. No independent human editorial review; not a complete exam chapter.

concepts.title: Declare initial conditions
concepts.text: The transfer-function model G(s)=K/(τs+1) below assumes zero initial state and τ>0. Its pole is −1/τ. Initial stored energy adds a response that the zero-state formula does not include.

concepts.title: Read gain and time constant
concepts.text: For a unit step, y(t)=K(1−exp(−t/τ)), t≥0. The final value is K. At one time constant, the response reaches about 63.2% of that final value, not 63.2% of one unit for every K.

concepts.title: Keep the feedback sign
concepts.text: For forward G and feedback H with negative feedback, closed-loop T=G/(1+GH). The characteristic denominator must be analysed after combining terms. The ideal formula does not certify real actuator stability or saturation limits.

example.problem: For G(s)=2/(s+2), find the time constant and final zero-state output for a unit step. Then find the unity-negative-feedback transfer function.
steps: Rewrite G(s)=1/(0.5 s+1), so K=1 and τ=0.5 s.
The pole is−2 s⁻¹ and the unit-step final output is 1.
Unity-negative feedback gives T=G/(1+G).
example.answer: Time constant 0.5 s; open-loop step final value 1; closed-loop T(s)=2/(s+4).

recall: Where does the pole lie for positiveτ?
Is K a time constant?
What changes for positive rather than negative feedback?
units.mistake: Do not readτ directly as the constant term of an unnormalised denominator. Final-value reasoning requires a stable applicable response.

units.title: Signals: calculate a finite convolution
units.subject: Signals and Systems
units.objective: A list of samples is incomplete without an origin. Here finite sequences start at n=0 and are zero elsewhere. State that before shifting or convolving.
units.review: Original worked lesson with author checks. No independent human editorial review; not a complete exam chapter.

concepts.title: Label time indices
concepts.text: A list of samples is incomplete without an origin. Here finite sequences start at n=0 and are zero elsewhere. State that before shifting or convolving.

concepts.title: Use the overlap sum
concepts.text: For a discrete-time LTI system, y[n]=Σk x[k]h[n−k]. Compute one n at a time; terms outside the finite support are zero.

concepts.title: Check length and total
concepts.text: For original x=[1,2] and h=[1,1], output is[1,3,2]. Full linear convolution has length 2+2−1=3. Its sum 6 equals(1+2)(1+1), a useful arithmetic check, not a substitute for every coefficient.

example.problem: For x[0]=2,x[1]=1 and h[0]=1,h[1]=−1, zero elsewhere, find the full linear convolution.
steps: The support is n=0,1,2 and the sum 0 equals(sum x)(sum h)=3×0.

recall: Why must the sample origin be stated?
What is the full output length?
How does the impulse response enter an LTI output?
units.mistake: This is linear convolution, not circular convolution or pointwise multiplication. Padding and wraparound change a circular-convolution problem.

units.title: Analog electronics: ideal op-amp feedback
units.subject: Analog Electronics
units.objective: Use the ideal voltage-feedback model only with stable negative feedback and unsaturated output. In that linear regime input currents are zero and input differential voltage tends to zero.
units.review: Original worked lesson with author checks. No independent human editorial review; not a complete exam chapter.

concepts.title: State the operating region
concepts.text: Use the ideal voltage-feedback model only with stable negative feedback and unsaturated output. In that linear regime input currents are zero and input differential voltage tends to zero.

concepts.title: Distinguish two circuits
concepts.text: An inverting amplifier has gain−Rf/Rin. A non-inverting amplifier has gain 1+Rf/Rg. Resistors are positive magnitudes; the inverting sign is part of the topology.

concepts.title: Verify the output limit
concepts.text: For an original inverting gain−5 and input 0.4 V, the predicted output is−2 V. If the available output swing cannot reach−2 V, the linear result is invalid. A virtual ground is not a physical current sink into the input terminal.

example.problem: An ideal inverting amplifier has Rin=10 kΩ, Rf=30 kΩ and Vin=0.5 V. Assume stable linear operation. Find gain, output and input-resistor current.
steps: The non-inverting input is grounded, so the inverting node is at virtual 0 V in the stated linear model.
Input-resistor current=(0.5−0)/10000=50 µA; it flows through the feedback resistor, not into the ideal input.
example.answer: Gain−3; Vout−1.5 V; resistor current 50 µA.

recall: When does virtual-ground reasoning apply?
Which configuration adds 1 to the resistor ratio?
Where does input-resistor current flow?
units.mistake: Zero differential input voltage is not guaranteed for open-loop operation or saturation. Do not use the virtual-short rule without the negative-feedback assumption.

units.title: Semiconductors: check a diode model consistently
units.subject: Analog Electronics
units.objective: An ideal conducting diode has zero voltage drop; a constant-drop model uses the stated forward drop. Neither model is a universal exact description of a real diode at all currents and temperatures.
units.review: Original worked lesson with author checks. No independent human editorial review; not a complete exam chapter.

concepts.title: Choose the model first
concepts.text: An ideal conducting diode has zero voltage drop; a constant-drop model uses the stated forward drop. Neither model is a universal exact description of a real diode at all currents and temperatures.

concepts.title: Test your assumed state
concepts.text: Assume on or off, solve the circuit, then check the implied voltage and current against the assumed direction. A contradiction means the assumed state is invalid.

concepts.title: Separate current and voltage
concepts.text: For an original 5 V source, a forward diode with prescribed 0.7 V drop and a 1 kΩ series resistor, I=(5−0.7)/1000=4.3 m A. The resistor, not the diode, carries the remaining 4.3 V drop.

example.problem: A 6 V DC source drives a correctly forward-oriented constant-drop diode and a 2 kΩ resistor in series. Use a 0.6 V diode drop. Find current and resistor power.
steps: Assume the diode is on in its prescribed forward direction.
The resistor voltage is 6−0.6=5.4 V.
Current is 5.4/2000=2.7 m A, consistent with forward conduction.
Resistor power isI²R=(0.0027)²×2000=0.01458 W.
example.answer: Current 2.7 m A; resistor power 14.58 m W.

recall: Why must a model be named?
How do you check an assumed on state?
Is 0.7 V an exact universal diode voltage?
units.mistake: An ideal diode and a 0.7 V constant-drop diode are different models. Reverse breakdown, leakage and heating need additional device information.

units.title: Measurements: distinguish bounds and standard uncertainty
units.subject: Measurements and Instrumentation
units.objective: A maximum error bound is not automatically a standard uncertainty. The combination rule depends on whether inputs are bounds, standard uncertainties or correlated estimates.
units.review: Original worked lesson with author checks. No independent human editorial review; not a complete exam chapter.

concepts.title: Name what ± means
concepts.text: A maximum error bound is not automatically a standard uncertainty. The combination rule depends on whether inputs are bounds, standard uncertainties or correlated estimates.

concepts.title: Propagate standard uncertainties
concepts.text: For independent inputs x,y with standard uncertainties ux,uy, a sum has combined standard uncertainty sqrt(ux²+uy²). A difference uses the same squared terms. Correlation adds covariance terms and cannot be ignored when present.

concepts.title: Keep worst-case bounds separate
concepts.text: For stated absolute bounds ax,ay, the worst-case bound on x+y is ax+ay. Original bounds 0.2 and 0.3 give 0.5; standard uncertainties 0.2 and 0.3 instead give approximately 0.361 when independent.

example.problem: Two independent measured quantities have standard uncertainties 3 and 4 in one common unit. Find the combined standard uncertainty of their sum. Compare with maximum bounds 3 and 4.
steps: For independent standard uncertainties use root-sum-square.
Compute sqrt(3²+4²)=sqrt 25=5 units.
If 3 and 4 were maximum absolute bounds, add magnitudes instead.
The corresponding worst-case bound would be 3+4=7 units; these describe different input assumptions.
example.answer: Combined standard uncertainty 5; corresponding sum of maximum bounds 7.

recall: Does ± always mean one standard deviation?
When does root-sum-square apply?
What information is missing for correlated inputs?
units.mistake: Do not silently interpret a manufacturer tolerance as a standard deviation, or use independence when the same instrument creates correlated errors.

units.title: Probability: condition on the right population
units.subject: Mathematics
units.objective: P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B) when P(B)>0. The denominator is the condition, not the whole original population.
units.review: Original worked lesson with author checks. No independent human editorial review; not a complete exam chapter.

concepts.title: Restrict the population
concepts.text: P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B) when P(B)>0. The denominator is the condition, not the whole original population.

concepts.title: Reconstruct counts
concepts.text: For an original machine-output example, machine A makes 60 items with 6 defective and B makes 40 with 2 defective. A random defective item comes from A with probability 6/(6+2)=3/4, not 60/100.

concepts.title: Test independence
concepts.text: A and B are independent when P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B). Mutually exclusive nonzero-probability events are not independent: their intersection is zero even though the product is positive.

example.problem: A box holds 30 red and 20 blue tokens. Of these,12 red and 8 blue are stamped. A token is selected uniformly from the box and is known to be stamped. Find the probability it is red.
steps: Restrict to stamped tokens:12+8=20.
The favourable stamped-red count is 12.
Conditional probability=12/20=0.6.
Check the event definition: selection is known stamped, so use 20 rather than 50 in the denominator.

recall: What event determines the denominator?
When is conditional probability undefined?
Are mutually exclusive nonzero events independent?
units.mistake: P(A|B) and P(B|A) generally differ. Selection bias or a changed sampling rule can invalidate a simple count ratio.

units.title: Ecology: classify interactions using evidence
units.subject: Environment
units.objective: Use a simplified interaction sign pair for the two species: mutualism(+,+), commensalism(+,0), competition(−,−) and exploitation such as parasitism(+ ,−). The label depends on the described effects.
units.review: Original worked lesson with author checks. No independent human editorial review; not a complete exam chapter.

concepts.title: Specify the two effects
concepts.text: Use a simplified interaction sign pair for the two species: mutualism(+,+), commensalism(+,0), competition(−,−) and exploitation such as parasitism(+ ,−). The label depends on the described effects.

concepts.title: Read the stated scenario
concepts.text: In an original hypothetical experiment, organism A gains food while B has lower survival. This supports a(+ ,−) interaction under those conditions. Merely observing two species together does not establish benefit or causation.

concepts.title: Avoid universal labels
concepts.text: Effects can vary with context and life stage. Use the problem’s observations rather than assuming every association is always beneficial or that one example describes all species in a group.

example.problem: In an invented controlled comparison, species A receives food from B and B receives protection from A. Both show improved survival compared with otherwise matched controls. Classify the interaction under the stated conditions.
steps: Identify the effect on A: food improves its survival, coded+.
Identify the effect on B: protection improves its survival, coded+.
The pair is(+,+), consistent with mutualism in this described comparison.
The result does not establish that the relationship is obligatory or identical in every environment.

recall: What evidence distinguishes commensalism from mutualism?
Does coexistence prove benefit?
Why can interaction labels depend on context?
units.mistake: Zero in a simplified sign model means no measured effect under stated conditions, not proof that every possible effect is exactly zero.

units.title: Geography: weather, climate and valid comparisons
units.subject: Geography
units.objective: Weather describes shorter-term atmospheric conditions. Climate concerns longer-term patterns and distributions. One unusual day does not on its own establish or refute a long-term trend.
units.review: Original worked lesson with author checks. No independent human editorial review; not a complete exam chapter.

concepts.title: Match the time scale
concepts.text: Weather describes shorter-term atmospheric conditions. Climate concerns longer-term patterns and distributions. One unusual day does not on its own establish or refute a long-term trend.

concepts.title: Use comparable records
concepts.text: A trend comparison should consider the same variable, location or defined region, observation method and period. Changing instruments or sampling coverage can require adjustment before interpreting differences.

concepts.title: Distinguish average and variability
concepts.text: In an original example, a fictional station has a baseline mean 20°C and a comparison-period mean 21°C, an anomaly of+1°C. This does not say every day was warmer by 1°C or that extremes were unchanged.

example.problem: A fictional station’s baseline mean temperature is 18°C and a later comparable period’s mean is 19.5°C. Find the mean anomaly and say what it does not prove.
steps: Keep the same station, variable and compatible observation method.
Anomaly=later mean−baseline mean=19.5−18=+1.5°C.
This is a difference in means, not a percentage temperature change.
It does not show that each individual day rose by 1.5°C, or attribute the change to one cause.
example.answer: +1.5°C mean anomaly; daily changes and causes are not established by these means alone.

recall: Can one cold day refute a long-term trend?
What must be comparable across records?
Does a mean describe every individual observation?
units.mistake: Percent change on the Celsius scale can be misleading because its zero is not absolute. Use the requested temperature difference and clearly specified units.

questions.stem: Find the determinant of [[4,1],[2,3]].
For 3 x+y=11 and x−y=1, find x.
questions.explanation: Adding gives 4 x=12, so x=3 and y=2.

questions.stem: Which statement about two identical linear equations in two unknowns is correct?
questions.explanation: Identical compatible equations impose one independent constraint.
options: The coefficient matrix must be invertible

questions.stem: For A=diag(2,7), find the eigenvalue corresponding to v=(0,3).
For a square matrix A with nonzero determinant, which statements hold?
questions.explanation: Invertibility gives a unique solution for every b; zero determinant does not occur here.
options: AX=b has one solution for every b

questions.stem: Find the trace of [[6,2],[1,−4]].
questions.explanation: The trace is the sum of diagonal entries:6−4=2.

questions.stem: For f(x)=x³−2 x, find f′(2).
Evaluate the definite integral of 3 x² from x=0 to x=2.
questions.explanation: The antiderivative is x³;2³−0=8.

questions.stem: For f(x)=5 x+2, find its derivative at x=7.
questions.explanation: The slope of this linear function is always 5.

questions.stem: A signed velocity is negative throughout an interval. Which statement must hold?
questions.explanation: The velocity integral is negative, while distance is positive.

questions.stem: Which derivative statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Differentiate term by term.

questions.stem: For v(t)=4 m/s constant on 0≤t≤5 s, find displacement in m.
For G(s)=4/(2 s+1), find the time constant in seconds.
questions.explanation: The denominator is alreadyτs+1, soτ=2 s.

questions.stem: For G(s)=3/(s+2), find its DC gain.
For G(s)=1/(0.25 s+1), find its pole in s⁻¹.
For a stable positive-gain first-order zero-state unit-step response, approximately what fraction of the final value is reached at t=τ?
For G(s)=K/(τs+1), τ>0 and zero initial state, which statements hold?
questions.explanation: The pole is negative and the DC gain is K; other claims confuse quantities.
options: The unit-step final value is K
The time constant always equals K

questions.stem: A static forward gain G=4 has unity negative feedback. Find the closed-loop gain.
For x=[1,2] and h=[1,1], find y[1].
questions.context: All finite sequences start at n=0 and are zero elsewhere. Use full linear convolution.

questions.stem: For x=[2,1] and h=[1,−1], find y[2].
questions.explanation: At n=2 only x[1]h[1]=−1 remains.
questions.context: All finite sequences start at n=0 and are zero elsewhere. Use full linear convolution.

questions.stem: Two finite sequences have lengths 4 and 3. What is the full linear convolution length?
questions.explanation: 4+3−1=6 samples.

questions.stem: Convolving a sequence x[n] with the unit impulse δ[n] gives which result?
questions.explanation: The impulse acts as the identity under convolution.

questions.stem: Which properties hold for full linear convolution of finite sequences?
questions.explanation: Reordering and association preserve convolution; pointwise multiplication is a different operation.
options: Its output always has the input length

questions.stem: For x=[3,1] and h=[2,2], find the sum of all full-convolution output samples.
questions.explanation: The output is[6,8,2], with sum 16=(3+1)(2+2).
questions.context: All finite sequences start at n=0 and are zero elsewhere. Use full linear convolution.

questions.stem: An ideal linear inverting amplifier has Rin=5 kΩ and Rf=20 kΩ. Find its voltage gain.
An ideal linear non-inverting amplifier has Rf=20 kΩ and Rg=10 kΩ. Find its gain.
An ideal linear inverting amplifier has gain−6 and input 0.2 V. Find output in V.
In the stated ideal op-amp model, what is the current into either input terminal?
questions.explanation: Infinite input impedance means zero input-terminal current.

questions.stem: Which conditions justify the virtual-short approximation for an ideal voltage-feedback op amp?
questions.explanation: Negative feedback and linear unsaturated operation are required.
options: The output remains within its linear operating range
Positive feedback always forces equal inputs

questions.stem: A 10 kΩ input resistor has 0.3 V across it in an ideal inverting circuit. Find its current in µA.
A 5 V source drives a forward-oriented 0.7 V constant-drop diode and 1 kΩ series resistor. Find current in m A.
A 9 V source drives an ideal forward-conducting diode and 3 kΩ series resistor. Find current in m A.
questions.explanation: The ideal on-state drop is 0 V, so 9/3000 A=3 m A.

questions.stem: Which statement about a quoted 0.7 V diode drop is correct?
questions.explanation: It is a chosen approximation for a problem, not a universal law.
options: It is exact for every diode
It makes current independent of the series resistor
It can be a stated constant-drop approximation
It proves reverse breakdown has occurred

questions.stem: A forward-biased diode has 0.6 V across it and carries 2 m A. Find diode power in m W.
Which steps belong to consistent piecewise diode analysis?
questions.explanation: State assumptions, solve and check consistency.
options: Check the solved current direction against the assumed state

questions.stem: A constant-drop diode of 0.5 V is in series with 1.5 kΩ across 5 V in the forward direction. Find current in m A.
Independent standard uncertainties are 3 and 4 V. Find the combined standard uncertainty of their sum in V.
questions.explanation: sqrt(3²+4²)=5 V.

questions.stem: Two additive quantities have maximum absolute error bounds 0.2 and 0.3 V. Find the worst-case bound on their sum in V.
questions.explanation: Worst-case absolute bounds add:0.2+0.3=0.5 V.

questions.stem: Which extra information matters when combining correlated standard uncertainties?
questions.explanation: Propagation must include covariance terms.
options: Only the colour of the instrument

questions.stem: Independent standard uncertainties are 6 and 8 mm. Find the combined standard uncertainty of their difference in mm.
questions.explanation: For independent inputs, variances add for a difference too: sqrt(36+64)=10 mm.

questions.stem: Which statements are valid?
questions.explanation: The numerical meaning of the inputs determines the combination method.
options: A maximum bound is not automatically a standard uncertainty
Worst-case bounds must always be combined by root-sum-square
Correlation can change combined standard uncertainty
All error sources are independent by definition

questions.stem: A measured 100 V quantity has a maximum absolute error bound 2 V. Find the bound as a percentage of the measured value.
Among 20 stamped tokens,12 are red. A uniformly selected stamped token is red with what probability?
Machine A contributes 6 defective items and B contributes 2. One item is selected uniformly from all defective items. Find the probability it came from A.
P(A∩B)=0.12 and P(B)=0.3. Find P(A|B).
Events A and B are mutually exclusive and each has positive probability. Are they independent?
questions.explanation: Their intersection is zero but P(A)P(B)>0.
options: Only if the sample space is finite

questions.stem: Which statements are correct for elementary conditional probability?
questions.explanation: Conditioning divides by the condition probability, and independence factors the intersection.
options: Mutually exclusive positive-probability events are independent

questions.stem: Independent events have probabilities 0.2 and 0.5. Find their intersection probability.
In a stated interaction, both species benefit. Which simplified label fits?
questions.explanation: The sign pair is(+,+), which defines mutualism in the simplified model.

questions.stem: Species A benefits while no effect on B is detected under the stated conditions. Which simplified label fits?
questions.explanation: The pair(+,0) describes commensalism.

questions.stem: Two species each have reduced growth when competing for the same limiting resource. Which sign pair describes the stated effects?
questions.explanation: Competition harms both relative to the defined comparison.

questions.stem: A parasite gains resources while its host is harmed. Which sign pair describes parasite,host?
questions.explanation: The parasite benefits and the host is harmed.

questions.stem: Which conclusions are justified from interaction evidence?
questions.explanation: Labels require stated effects and may depend on context.
options: Measured benefit to both can support mutualism under those conditions
The same association can have different effects in different environments
A simplified zero effect proves absolutely no possible effect

questions.stem: Two species are observed at the same site, with no measurements of effects. What can be concluded about mutualism?
questions.explanation: Presence together does not measure benefits or establish interaction type.
options: It is not established by coexistence alone

questions.stem: A fictional station has a baseline mean 18°C and later comparable mean 19.5°C. Find later-minus-baseline anomaly in°C.
Which observation alone is insufficient to refute a long-term warming trend?
questions.explanation: An individual weather event does not determine a long-term distribution or trend.
options: A defined analysis of long-term means

questions.stem: Which comparison is most defensible for assessing a change in a station’s mean temperature?
questions.explanation: Compare the same variable and comparable periods using compatible records.
options: Comparable records of the same variable at that station
One indoor reading versus one outdoor reading
January at one site versus July at another without context
An unknown instrument reading with no date

questions.stem: A fictional station’s comparable mean is 17°C versus a 20°C baseline. Find the anomaly in°C.
Which statements correctly distinguish averages and individual conditions?
questions.explanation: A mean describes a collection and does not force identical changes in every element.
options: A mean increase need not mean every day increased equally
A mean alone identifies the only cause of change
Climate comparisons need a defined time scale
One hot afternoon determines the long-term climate

questions.stem: Two means differ by 2°C. Which statement is justified from that fact alone?
questions.explanation: Only the specified difference follows; distribution and cause require more evidence.
options: The difference of those means is 2°C
